newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian moves to free up gold industry as prices plunge.
newsitem.headline: Russian moves to free up gold industry as prices plunge.

text.p: Russia said Tuesday it was moving to free up its promising gold mining industry, but admitted the timing could not be worse after gold prices dropped to 12-year lows.

"Look where the problem is -- the world market price for gold is falling quickly," Central Bank Deputy Chairman Alexander Potyomkin said. "In dollar equivalent terms, the price has already killed mining costs in (our) far-flung regions."

Russia, the world's fifth largest gold producer with the third largest reserves in the ground, is struggling to reverse a slump in production by making it attractive for banks to lend money to mines to finance their output.

Potyomkin said President Boris Yeltsin would soon sign a long-awaited decree allowing banks to export precious metals -- a key step toward making it worth their while to finance gold output at home, where demand is limited.
But Russia still keeps a tight rein on the amount of gold banks can buy, and officials said the decree would not flood markets since banks held only 5 metric tons.
"What can 5 tons do to the market, which can easily digest such volumes?" asked Sergei Kyshtymov, head of the Central Bank of Russia's precious metals department.
The world price of gold has crumpled to around $320 an ounce on recent sales by Australia's central bank.
"Now our gold will just sit in the ground," said Viktor Tarakanovsky, board chairman of Russia's Gold Prospectors' Union.

Private Russian citizens can now buy and sell small amounts of gold on the domestic market, and cash-strapped Moscow has said banks and foreign and domestic investors are key to tapping big Siberian reserves.
Russia's gold industry is still more politically than economically driven, with Moscow slow to allow changes in an industry that brings it billions of dollars.
Officials see Russia's 1997 gold output in the range of 95 to 110 tons, down from 124 tons in 1996.
"Fifty percent of gold is mined beyond the Arctic Circle, but the price of electricity, heat, fuel is several times higher," Kyshtymov said. "The mines become uncompetitive."
